This page goes with **Chapter 33, Set Theory** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SetTheory.html). Read each section there first.
Set theory describes music that does not use chords and keys in the old way (the book's example is Webern's Op. 5 No. 3), so the tools
here work on bare pitch classes. Every answer on this page is computed by the same code the calculator uses, and a test checks that code
against all 208 set classes of three to nine notes in the book's tables.

## 33.1 Pitch-class integers

A **pitch class** is a note with its octave forgotten, and with enharmonic spellings merged: C&sharp; and D&flat; are one pitch class.
Number them from C = 0 up to B = 11. Ten and eleven are written **T** and **E** so that a set stays one character per note.
Intervals are counted the same way: the distance from 2 to 9 is 7 semitones. Because 12 is the same as 0, arithmetic is "modulo 12".

The clock face below puts C at the top. Click points to build a set, or type pitch classes ("0 4 7").

## 33.2 The calculator

::: {.pt data-pt="setcalc" data-set="0 4 7"}
:::

Start with the presets. Notice that a major and a minor triad get the **same** prime form and Forte name, 3-11: set theory counts them as one *set class*.

## 33.3 Normal form

The **normal form** of a set is the way of writing its notes in ascending order that is the most compact. Rules, in this site's words:

1. List the pitch classes once each, in ascending order.
2. Rotate the list so that each note takes a turn at the start, wrapping the low notes up an octave.
3. Choose the rotation whose first and last notes are closest together.
4. If two rotations tie, choose the one that is more tightly packed at the start (compare the first note to the next-to-last, then to the one before that, and so on). Last tie-break: the lower first note.

Try: B&flat;, C, D&flat;, E&flat; is [T 0 1 3] (not [0 1 3 T]), because T up to 3 spans 5 semitones and no other starting point does better.

## 33.4 Prime form

The **prime form** moves the normal form so it starts on 0, and also does the same to the *inversion* of the set; the more tightly packed
of the two wins. It is the name of the whole set class: every transposition and inversion of a set shares it. It is written in
parentheses, such as (037). The book uses Rahn's rule for ties; Forte's own rule differs for six classes (5-20, 6-Z29, 6-31, 7-Z18, 7-20, 8-26),
and the page's tables follow the book.

## 33.5 Interval vector

The **interval vector** counts the interval classes (1 to 6) between every pair of notes in the set, written as six digits. Interval class
means an interval and its inversion are the same (a perfect fifth counts as a perfect fourth, class 5). The tritone, class 6, is counted once.
The vector of (037) is &lang;001110&rang;: one minor third (class 3), one major third (4), one perfect fourth/fifth (5), and no seconds.
A set of the same size and the same vector but a different prime form is **Z-related** (the Forte names have a Z: 4-Z15 and 4-Z29).

## 33.6 Forte names, and all the set classes

A **Forte name** is two numbers: the number of notes and the position of the class in Forte's list, such as 3-11 or 6-35.
Open any class from the list below and it loads into the calculator.

::: {.pt data-pt="setbrowser"}
:::

## 33.7 Transposition and inversion

T<sub>n</sub> adds n to every pitch class. T<sub>n</sub>I first inverts (turns each note x into 12 &minus; x) and then adds n. The
calculator's lower controls apply both to whatever is on the clock. To find n between two sets of the same class that are inversions of
each other, add their notes in opposite order: the book's [2,4,5] and [2,3,5] are related by T<sub>7</sub>I (2+5, 4+3, 5+2 all give 7).

## Practice

Find the prime form and Forte name by hand, then check yourself in the calculator or the quiz.

1. [2, 4, 5]
2. G, B, D
3. B&flat;, C, D&flat;, E&flat;
4. [0, 1, 5, 6]
5. A, C, E, F
6. [3, 4, 7, 8]

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

1. normal form [2 4 5]; prime form (013), 3-2, vector &lang;111000&rang;.
2. 7, 11, 2: normal form [7 E 2]; prime form (037), 3-11.
3. 10, 0, 1, 3: normal form [T 0 1 3]; prime form (0235), 4-10.
4. normal form [0 1 5 6]; prime form (0156), 4-8, vector &lang;200121&rang;.
5. 9, 0, 4, 5: normal form [4 5 9 0]; prime form (0158), 4-20.
6. normal form [3 4 7 8]; prime form (0145), 4-7.
:::

## For teachers

- The maths is in `apps/shared/post-tonal/pcset.js`; the test `node tests/post-tonal/pcset.test.js` checks every prime form, vector and
  Forte name against the book's tables and by enumerating all subsets (`NEG=1` must fail). It found three misprinted vectors in the book's
  tables (5-13, 6-2, 6-Z43); the page uses the counted ones.
- The text is written for the site, not copied from the book. Forte and Rahn are cited as the sources of the numbering and the prime-form rule; neither was re-read.
